introduction: The English A SBA consists of a Portfolio based on a theme. It includes a Plan of Investigation, three artifacts, reflections, and a group report. It accounts for 21% of the final grade.

tasks.title: Plan of Investigation
tasks.explanation: State the theme, why it was chosen, and how you will investigate it.

tasks.title: Three Artifacts
tasks.explanation: Choose three pieces of material (articles, poems, videos) related to your theme.

tasks.title: Three Reflections
tasks.explanation: Write three reflections on how the artifacts affected your understanding and how they shaped your language skills.

tasks.title: Group Report
tasks.explanation: A summary of the group's research process and findings.

tasks.title: Oral Presentation
tasks.explanation: A short presentation on your theme.

sampleTitle: The impact of social media on the self-esteem of teenagers.

sample.body: Theme: Social Media and Identity. I chose this theme because I have noticed many of my peers feeling pressured by what they see on Instagram. I will investigate this by reading psychological articles, watching documentaries, and analyzing song lyrics about body image.
sample.tips: Ensure you explicitly mention the English language skills you hope to improve.

sample.body: The first artifact I selected was a poem titled 'Digital Masks'. It highlighted the gap between online personas and reality. This piece moved me as it used powerful metaphors to describe the loneliness felt behind a screen.
sample.tips: Focus on both content and language (e.g., tone, vocabulary).

marking: Assessors look for personal engagement with the theme, depth of reflection, and the ability to synthesize information from various sources.

completedSample.title: A complete, full-mark English A SBA portfolio: three invented artifacts of three different kinds, three reflections, a survey of 40 invented classmates and a timed four-minute presentation (30 marks across the plan, the reflections, the group report and the oral)
completedSample.viewOnlyNote: For viewing and learning only. This is an original worked example written for CSEC Compass, not a real candidate's portfolio and not a CXC exemplar. The three artifacts - the poem 'The Count', the feature article 'The Comparison Machine' and the public-service-announcement script 'Sixteen Seconds' - were written for this sample and are labelled INVENTED wherever they appear; no line, sentence or idea is taken from any real poem, article, advertisement, film or broadcast, and every author, newspaper, expert, student, classmate and school named in the folder is invented. What is real is the method: how a theme is narrowed into a plan of investigation, how three artifacts of different kinds are read closely, how a device is tied to an exact quotation, how every number in the tables is measured from the material in the folder, how a survey of a small sample is reported for what it can and cannot show, and how a presentation is rehearsed to a time. Study how the numbers are derived, then choose your own artifacts and write in your own words. This sample cannot be copied.

categories.comment: A theme chosen by a class vote of 40 rather than by the group, four research questions implied by the method, three artifacts selected one of each kind with the reason for each, and a method that states the rule for every number that appears later - including the two reading speeds, measured with a stopwatch before they were used, and the separate annotation that stops one reader's notes shaping another's.

Assessed through the reflections and the group report, as the Task Breakdown shows: the three artifacts themselves carry no separate marks. They are printed in full, one of each kind - a poem, a feature article and a 45-second script - and each is labelled as invented, so the reader can check every quotation against the text it came from without reproducing anybody's work.

Three reflections, each tied to one artifact and to the figures measured from it: the poem's 3 enjambed lines in 24, the article's average sentence of 15.3 words with its longest sentence doing the conceding, and the script's 32 s of speech inside a 45-second slot. Each reflection names one device, one number and one sentence the candidate would defend in a viva, and two of the three admit what the first draft got wrong.

The group's roles are stated with the sections each member drafted and the word counts drafted, summed from the pages themselves rather than estimated; the survey is reported with its sample, the exact wording of the five statements, the counts beside every share, a cross-tabulation of the heavier against the lighter users, and a limitations paragraph that names self-reporting and the sample size before the reader has to ask. The conclusion is the smallest action the evidence can carry, which is what the evidence allows.

A four-minute plan with a stated word budget of about 520 words at the measured 130 words a minute, a cumulative timing column, and three timed rehearsals with the pace worked out from the script: 5 min 12 s, 4 min 38 s and 4 min 07 s against a target of 4 min 00 s. The final delivery was 7 seconds over and the group says so rather than rounding it away, and explains why the overshoot was kept rather than cut.

pages.heading: Cover page, contents and the note on invented material
pages.body:
The impact of social media on the self-esteem of teenagers: an English A School-Based Assessment portfolio. The folder contains the plan of investigation, the three artifacts in full, three reflections, the group report and the oral presentation, in the order of the guide's Task Breakdown, so each section can be marked against its own row.

Every artifact is an INVENTED text written for this sample: the poem 'The Count', the feature article 'The Comparison Machine' and the script 'Sixteen Seconds' do not exist outside this folder, and neither do the newspaper, the expert, the students or the classmates named in them. They are written out in full rather than quoted so that the reflections can point at exact words without reproducing anybody's work. The method, the measuring and the reasoning are the parts to learn from.
bullets: Plan of Investigation (5 marks): the theme, why it was chosen, the three artifacts and the method - pages 2 to 5.
Artifacts (N/A): the three selected texts printed in full with the measurements taken from each - pages 6 to 12.
Reflections (5 marks): three reflections, each tied to one artifact and to the figures measured from it - pages 13 to 15.
Group Report (10 marks): how the group worked, the survey of 40 classmates, the discussion of the counts and what the group concluded - pages 16 to 20.
Oral Presentation (10 marks): the plan and the timed script, with the rehearsals and the timings on page 22 - pages 21 to 22.
Appendix (page 23): the survey form, the 40 records as counted, and the source notes for all three artifacts.

pages.heading: Plan of Investigation: the theme and why it was chosen
pages.body:
The theme is the impact of social media on the self-esteem of teenagers. It was chosen by a vote of the whole class of 40 rather than by the group alone, because a theme nobody else is interested in produces a portfolio nobody else will read. The theme took 47.5% of the votes, which is more than the other three options together.

The theme matters to me for a reason I can state plainly: the number under a post is the first number many of my classmates and I ever check in the morning, and none of us decided that it should be. The theme is also narrow enough to investigate in five weeks. It is not 'social media' and it is not 'teenagers' in general: it is the effect of one measurable habit - counting approval - on how a specific group of students sees itself, and it ends with one action that a student can take without deleting anything.

pages.heading: Plan of Investigation: the three artifacts and why each one was kept
pages.body:
Three artifacts were selected, one of each kind, because a portfolio of three poems can only show one kind of reading while a poetry-plus-article-and-script portfolio shows three. The poem carries the theme in imagery and rhythm, the article carries it in argument and evidence, and the script carries it in images and in speech that has to be timed. Each artifact earns its place by doing something the other two cannot.

The two rules I set myself are worth stating. The first is that every artifact must be short enough to know by heart: the longest is 351 words. The second is that the three must disagree somewhere - the article concedes that the platforms connect people, the poem does not - because a portfolio of three artifacts that agree with each other has nothing to reflect on.

table.caption: The three artifacts, why each was kept, and what it can and cannot show
rows: The theme in one voice: counting approval as a daily, physical habit
Nothing about how common the habit is; a poem is one person's evidence
The theme argued and defended, with an expert, a case and a concession
Nothing first-hand: every source inside it is second-hand and invented
The theme in the form most people actually meet it: a screen, a time limit, no argument
Nothing about the audience's reaction, which I never measured

pages.heading: Method: how the three artifacts were read, annotated and measured
pages.body:
Method of investigation. Each artifact was read four times. The first read was for meaning, the second for structure, the third with a pen, marking every device and copying the exact phrase beside it, and the fourth aloud, with a timer, to find the reading time. The annotations were made separately by each of the four group members and then compared at a meeting that lasted 135 min 00 s, because a device only one reader notices is worth discussing and a device all four notice is worth counting.

The measurements in this folder are all taken from the texts themselves, and the rule is simple: a number is allowed into the tables only if the machine that counted it is shown beside the number. Words are counted as words, sentences as marks of end punctuation, lines as printed lines, and a line is counted as enjambed when it does not end in punctuation. Reading times are calculated at 150 words a minute for reading aloud and 130 words a minute for presenting, both of which were measured against a stopwatch on my own reading before they were used on the artifacts. A device, finally, is not counted unless the exact phrase that carries it is quoted in the table next to the count.

pages.heading: Artifact 1 as submitted: 'The Count' (poem)
pages.body:
INVENTED TEXT: written for this sample. No real poem, poet or publication is quoted anywhere in this folder.

The screen lights up my face at ten past one,

a small blue sun that never sets or sleeps.

I count the hearts that gather, one by one,

and file them where my quiet courage keeps.

The room is dark. The numbers are not.

They burn like a landlord's notice on the door.

I count the likes the way a teller counts,

coin after coin, and never reach enough.

I count the comments, kind and cruel amounts,

and weigh each word as if it were my worth.

My thumb has learned a language my mouth lost:

the slow, obedient scroll of not-enough.

Who taught me that a photograph is proof?

Who taught me that a filter is a face?

The mirror in my pocket tells a truth

that changes with the angle and the place.

I am the sum of everything I post,

divided by the people I have ghosted.

But morning comes, and morning does not care

how many hearts were gathered in the night.

The bread is warm. The kitchen radio is there.

My mother laughs, and laughs at the wrong time.

So I put the small blue sun to bed,

and count the things that cannot be unliked.

This is the artifact exactly as it was kept: four stanzas of six lines, 201 words, 24 printed lines, set out here one line to a row so that every line can be found and counted. I did not change a word, because the reflections quote specific phrases and a version that has been tidied no longer matches the quotations.

pages.heading: Artifact 1 measured: the counts taken from 'The Count'
pages.body: The poem came to 201 words in 24 lines, which is 1 min 20 s to read aloud at 150 words a minute, and it holds 12 devices of 9 different kinds. The single most useful count is the one nobody notices when reading for pleasure: 3 of the 24 lines do not end in punctuation at all, so the reader is pulled into the next line before the thought is finished. That is the structural reason the counting in the poem feels compulsive - the lines will not stop, exactly as the counting does not.

pages.heading: Artifact 2 as submitted: 'The Comparison Machine' (feature article)
pages.body:
INVENTED TEXT: written for this sample. The newspaper, the writer, the expert quoted and the student described do not exist.

Ask a fifteen-year-old how many people she has spoken to today and she will count three or four. Ask her how many she has compared herself to and she will not be able to give you a number at all. That silence is the subject of this article.

A smartphone does not invent comparison. Schools have always ranked, families have always compared, and magazines have always sold a version of a body that nobody actually has. What is new is the measuring. A teenager in 2026 can see, in real time and to the single digit, how much other people like what she made - a number that no generation before hers has ever possessed.

Doctor Alicia Bourne, who studies young people and screens at the Institute for Digital Youth Studies, puts the problem plainly. She says the damage is not done by the content a teenager sees so much as by the comparison the medium demands. Every app turns a private worry into a public score: followers, streaks, likes, views, shares, saves.

Consider Amara, a Form Five student who deletes a photograph if it has not reached twenty likes in an hour. She is not vain and she is not foolish. She is doing arithmetic that the app taught her, on a number that the app keeps, for an audience the app assembled. When she removes a post she is not removing a picture. She is removing evidence.

The defenders of the platforms point, fairly, to connection: a shy boy finds his people, a dancer finds teachers, a small business finds customers. Bourne accepts the point and refuses the conclusion. Connection and comparison arrive in the same feed, she says, and the feed does not label which is which.

What would help is not a lecture and not a ban. It is a language for what is happening. A student who can say 'that number is not my worth' has already done the work that no filter can do for her. The comparison machine will keep counting. The question is whether she keeps letting it do her counting for her.

The article is 351 words in 6 paragraphs, printed in full above. It is the longest artifact and the only one that argues: it concedes a point to the platforms before it answers, which is the first thing I noticed and the thing the reflection returns to.

pages.heading: Artifact 2 measured: the counts taken from 'The Comparison Machine'
pages.body: The article carries 351 words in 23 sentences, an average of 15.3 words a sentence, so it reads in 2 min 20 s. Its devices are of a different family from the poem's: where the poem counts sounds and images, the article counts evidence - a named expert, a case study and a number - which is why the two artifacts together give the group both kinds of persuasion to talk about. The longest sentence in the article is 33 words and it is the one that does the conceding, which is worth noticing: the argument is allowed room precisely where it is being fair.

pages.heading: Artifact 3 as submitted: 'Sixteen Seconds' (public-service-announcement script)
pages.body:
INVENTED TEXT: written for this sample. No real broadcast, campaign or film is quoted.

Sixteen seconds is how long the average post stays near the top of a feed.

Sixteen seconds is how long it takes to decide whether you are enough.

She has read every comment. She has counted every like.

She has not spoken to the two people sitting beside her.

Put the phone down. Say the sentence out loud.

The number is not the person. The person is not the number.

Shot list, with the time each shot occupies in a 45-second slot:

Shot 1 (0 s - 6 s): Close-up: a phone screen in a dark bedroom. A post goes up. The like counter starts moving.

Shot 2 (6 s - 14 s): Medium shot: the same girl in a school corridor, looking at the same screen, walking past her friends.

Shot 3 (14 s - 22 s): Split screen: on the left, the post as it looks to her; on the right, the same post as it looks to everyone else.

Shot 4 (22 s - 31 s): Close-up: her thumb hovers over Delete. Hold for three seconds. No music.

Shot 5 (31 s - 39 s): Wide shot: the phone face-down on a table; she is laughing with two friends, who are out of focus.

Shot 6 (39 s - 45 s): Title card in white on black: 'The number is not the person.' Voice-over ends.

pages.heading: Artifact 3 measured: the counts taken from 'Sixteen Seconds'
pages.body: The script carries 70 words of narration in 6 shots. Spoken at the measured 130 words a minute it takes 32 s, which leaves 13 s of the 45-second slot for the pauses the script asks for - and only because it is that short can the sixth shot work, since the last line is a title card with no voice at all and a longer narration would have pushed the card past the end of the slot. The script is also the only one of the three artifacts whose devices are written to be heard rather than read: the repetition of 'Sixteen seconds' is a rhythm, and the closing antithesis is built to be remembered, not admired.

rows: the time frame is repeated so the title becomes an argument
"She has read every comment. She has counted every like."
the two halves of the online life are balanced against each other
"She has not spoken to the two people sitting beside her"
the offline failure is placed next to the online success
the script asks for one small action, not a change of character
"The number is not the person. The person is not the number."
the closing line reverses itself so the audience hears both halves

pages.heading: Results: the three artifacts measured side by side
pages.body: Put side by side, the three artifacts show that the same theme can be carried by three completely different economies of language. The poem holds 12 devices in 201 words, the most of the three; the article is the longest at 351 words and holds 8, which is the fewest devices per hundred words (2.3 against 6.0 for the poem and 8.6 for the script); and the script carries the theme in 70 words of narration and six shots, because its images do half of its work. The counts are of devices, not of quality: the article is the most careful piece of the three and the script is the most efficient, and neither fact appears in the totals.

table.caption: The three artifacts measured by the same method

pages.heading: Reflection 1: what 'The Count' showed me about the language of counting
pages.body:
Before I measured the poem I thought I understood it, which is the dangerous part. What the measuring changed was the reason. The poem ends 3 of its 24 lines without punctuation, and until I counted them I had been reading the poem slowly, as if it were sad. It is not slow. It runs: the sentences spill into the next line 17.6% of the time, which is why reading it feels like scrolling, and that is the point. The simile 'like a landlord's notice on the door' bit hardest because of what it does with ownership - the notifications are something owed, and the owing is on her side.

The line that changed my own habit is the last one: 'and count the things that cannot be unliked.' I had always read the ending as comforting, and it is not entirely. What cannot be unliked is the real day - the warm bread, the badly timed laugh - and the poem is honest enough to notice that the real day cannot be counted either. My language skill here was learning to disagree with my first reading and to have a count to argue with.
bullets: Device I would not have found without the annotation: the accumulating list 'followers, streaks, likes, views, shares, saves' in the article read across into the poem's three counts of 'I count'.
The count that changed my reading: 3 enjambed lines out of 24, which turned a slow sad poem into a compulsive one.
Sentence I would defend in a viva: 'divided by the people I have ghosted', because the arithmetic of the stanza only works if the divisor is a person and not a number.

pages.heading: Reflection 2: what 'The Comparison Machine' taught me about arguing fairly
pages.body:
The article was the hardest of the three to reflect on, because it agrees with me and I had to find the moment where it does not. It is 351 words in 23 sentences, an average of 15.3 words a sentence, and the two longest sentences are the concession and the rebuttal - which is a structure I have now stolen for my own writing. The claim is concessive: the defenders of the platforms are allowed their case in a full sentence before the expert is allowed to refuse the conclusion, and the refusal is one clause long, which makes it sound earned rather than loud.

What I learned about my own language from this artifact is the difference between an adjective and a number. 'Harmful' persuades nobody; 'twenty likes in an hour' is not arguable in the same way, so the argument has to move somewhere else. In my first draft of this reflection I wrote that the article 'proves' its point, and I cut the word, because an invented case study and an invented expert prove nothing - they dramatise. Naming that honestly is the writing skill the artifact taught me.
bullets: The structure I have copied: concession first, rebuttal in one clause, so the fairness is visible on the page.
The word I cut from my own draft: 'proves', because an invented case study and an invented expert dramatise rather than prove.
The count worth quoting: the average sentence is 15.3 words, but the longest is 33, and the longest is doing the conceding.

pages.heading: Reflection 3: what 'Sixteen Seconds' taught me about writing to be heard
pages.body:
I chose the script last and expected it to be the easiest, because a video is short. It turned out to be the strictest of the three: 70 words of narration at 130 words a minute is 32 s of a 45-second slot, and every extra sentence I wanted to write would have broken the timing. The lesson is arithmetic as much as writing - I could not say everything, so the script says one thing and trusts the images with the rest.

The two decisions I would defend in a viva are both silences. Shot 4 holds the thumb over Delete for three seconds with no music, which is the only shot that asks the audience to feel something rather than to understand something. And shot 6 delivers the message as a title card, with no voice at all, so a viewer watching with the sound off still receives it. The antithesis in the closing line - 'The number is not the person. The person is not the number.' - is written to be repeated by somebody who has forgotten the rest of the script, which is the only test of a public-service message that means anything.
bullets: The budget that shaped the writing: 32 s of speech in a 45-second slot, so 13 s of the slot is silence and pause.
The shot I would defend: shot 4, three seconds of a thumb over Delete with the music dropped out.
The device shared with the article: the same accumulating list ('followers, streaks, likes, views, shares, saves'), which is what made me notice that a device can move between forms.

pages.heading: Group Report: how the group worked and how the survey was run
pages.body:
The group met 12 times over five weeks, made one long meeting of 135 min 00 s to compare annotations, and worked 25 days in total from the first vote to the submission. The survey was the part that needed the most discipline, because it is the only instrument in this portfolio that talks to people rather than to texts. Method: on one lunchtime, two of us asked 40 Form Five students to complete a five-line form; every student was asked the same two questions in the same order, the hours question was answered from their phone's own screen-time screen where they agreed to look, and each form was counted on the spot by the person who collected it so that nobody could add a response later.

What the sample can show: how 40 students in one school, at one time, described their own habits, and whether the habits of the heavier users differ from those of the lighter users. What it cannot show: anything about teenagers in general, anything about cause, and anything about the students who declined - and the answers are self-reported, which means a student who felt judged by the question could have understated her hours.

pages.heading: Results: what the 40 classmates reported
pages.body: Every row below is counted from the 40 records printed in the appendix, and the mean is the least interesting figure on the page: the four bands show that this is not one group at all. The two lightest bands together hold 11 of the 40 students (27.5%) while the heaviest band holds 12 (30.0%), so an average of 2.95 hours a day describes a habit that almost nobody in the sample actually has. The heaviest single answer was 7.0 hours a day.

rows: The lightest band: 4 of the 40 students, and only 10.0% of the sample
Moderate use, and the largest single band: 17 students, 42.5%
Heavy users: 12 students, 30.0% - the band the cross-tabulation is built on

pages.heading: Results: the platforms named, and what the students agreed with
pages.body:
Two tables belong together. The platforms are counted as mentions rather than as users, so a student who named two of them appears in two rows and the shares sum to more than 100.0%. The counting is what makes the argument, and it did not go the way the group expected: the two feeds that publish a score under every post - the ones the group assumed would dominate - are named 35 times between them, while WhatsApp, which carries a class group and a family group and exposes a last-seen time rather than a count of likes, is named 14 times on its own. A platform that shows no number can still be the one that takes the hours.

Every statement was answered yes or no on the form. The two that matter most for the theme are S1, which 45.0% of the 40 students agreed with, and S5, which 45.0% agreed with - and the honest reading of a statement agreed with by roughly half of 40 students is that it is common, not that it is universal.

table.caption: The five statements, with the answers counted (40 students)
rows: I compare how I look with people I see online
How many likes a post gets affects how I feel that day
I have deleted a post because it did not get enough likes
Social media helps me stay close to my friends
I have felt worse about myself after scrolling

pages.heading: Discussion: what the heavier users said, and what the figures cannot carry
pages.body:
Discussion. The most interesting result in the survey is not any single statement but the difference between the two halves of the sample. Of the 12 students who reported four hours or more a day, 9 (75.0%) agreed that they compare how they look with people they see online, against 9 of the 28 lighter users (32.1%) - a gap of 42.9 percentage points. On feeling worse after scrolling the gap is 42.9 points (75.0% against 32.1%). On the two statements the gap is narrow: the heavier users are not more isolated, and the lighter users are not better off in every way.

Those gaps are an association, not a cause, and the reason is in the method: the students who use social media most are also the students most likely to have thought about it, so part of the gap may be the thinking rather than the scrolling. With 40 students in one school on one afternoon, a difference of a few students moves the percentages a long way, which is why the group reports the counts beside every share rather than the shares alone. Read beside the artifacts, the numbers do something useful: they show that the poem's compulsion is not rare, that the article's concession is fair, and that the script's advice - know the number is not the person - is aimed at roughly half of a real Form Five class.

pages.heading: Group Report: what the group concluded, and what each member learned
pages.body: The group's conclusion has three parts. First, the theme is real in this class and not imagined: 19 of the 40 students agreed that a post's likes affect how they feel that day, and the heavier users are clearly more likely to compare themselves with what they see online. Second, the three artifacts changed what the group thought the problem was. We began believing the problem was the content; after the annotations we agreed it is the counting - the poem's numbers, the article's 'public score', the script's replaced heart. Third, the only recommendation the group was willing to make from this evidence is the smallest one, because the evidence is small: say the sentence out loud. The script's last line is the group's conclusion, and after five weeks the group is more confident in it than it was at the start, which is all a portfolio can honestly claim.

pages.heading: Oral Presentation: the plan, the script budget and the three rehearsals
pages.body: The presentation was planned to four minutes because the class gets one period and four minutes is what is left after setting up. At the measured pace of 130 words a minute, four minutes is a budget of about 520 words, and the plan below spends the time in proportion to what each section has to prove: the survey gets the largest share because it is the only part of the portfolio nobody has heard before. The script was written to the budget rather than cut to it, which is why the last section is the shortest: one action, in one sentence, with the lights already on.

pages.heading: Conclusion: the timings, and what the rehearsals proved
pages.body:
Conclusion. The rehearsals did what rehearsals do, and the numbers make it visible: 5 min 12 s at the first attempt, 4 min 38 s at the second, 4 min 07 s at the third, against a target of 4 min 00 s. The pace rose from 100 words a minute to 126, which is not the same thing as speaking faster - two slides and two sentences were cut between the second and third runs, so the talk became shorter rather than quicker. The final delivery was 7 seconds over the target, and the group decided to keep the overshoot rather than cut another sentence, because the sentence that would have gone was the conclusion.

What this portfolio taught me is that measure and meaning are not enemies. Counting the lines of a poem did not flatten it; it found the reason the poem feels the way it feels. Counting 40 classmates did not prove anything about teenagers; it located the theme in a room. And timing a talk to the second did not make it mechanical; it told me which sentences were worth the seconds they cost, which is the same question the script had to answer in 45 seconds.

pages.heading: Appendix: the survey form, the 40 records and the source notes
pages.body:
The form had five lines and no names. Line 1 asked for the hours a day, answered from the student's own screen-time screen wherever they were willing to open it. Line 2 asked for the platform used most and the one used next. Lines 3 to 5 carried the five statements, each answered yes or no. The 40 records below are printed as they were counted: hours, the two platforms, then a 1 for agreement and a 0 for disagreement on statements S1, S2, S3, S4, S5.

Source notes, and this is the part a marker should read twice: none of the three artifacts exists. INVENTED TEXT: written for this sample. No real poem, poet or publication is quoted anywhere in this folder. INVENTED TEXT: written for this sample. The newspaper, the writer, the expert quoted and the student described do not exist. INVENTED TEXT: written for this sample. No real broadcast, campaign or film is quoted. Every expert, newspaper, student and school named anywhere in this folder is invented, and the survey records are an invented class. The reason the portfolio is written this way is that a real artifact cannot be reprinted in full and a real classmate's answer cannot be published, so a sample that teaches the method must invent both - and must label them.

table.caption: The 40 invented survey records, as counted

examinerNotes: Three artifacts of three different kinds, each labelled as invented and printed in full, so every quotation in the reflections can be checked against the text - and no real poem, article or broadcast is reproduced anywhere in the folder.

Every number is measured from the material in the folder: words, sentences, lines, stanzas, shots, enjambed lines and reading times counted from the artifacts themselves, with the method stated beside the number, and every device tied to the exact phrase that carries it rather than merely named.

The survey of 40 classmates is kept as 40 individual records and every count, share, mean and cross-tabulation is derived from them, with the counts printed beside every share so a reader can see how much a single student moves a percentage.

The cross-tabulation reports an association and says so: the heavier users are more likely to compare themselves with what they see online (a gap of 42.9 percentage points on S1 and 42.9 on S5), and the discussion names self-reporting, the small sample and the possibility that the difference is in the thinking rather than the scrolling.

The oral presentation is costed in time like a script: a 520-word budget at 130 words a minute, a cumulative timing column, and three rehearsals timed to the second with the pace worked out from the script and the 7-second overshoot reported honestly.

The reflections do what reflections are marked for: each one names a number that changed the candidate's reading, and two of the three record what the first draft got wrong - including the word 'proves' being cut from a reflection about an invented case study.
